name: stp
desc: Simple Theorem Prover, an efficient SMT solver for bitvectors
why: An SMT solver for bitvectors is a real piece of logic machinery you can poke at, though it is niche and academic.

brief.what_it_is: STP is a command-line and library constraint solver (an SMT solver) for quantifier-free theories of bitvectors, arrays, floating-point, and linear real arithmetic. It takes a problem as an SMT-LIB2 file or on standard input, and prints whether the problem is satisfiable or unsatisfiable, with a model when satisfiable. It also has C, C++, and Python APIs for embedding it in other tools. The docs say its SMT-LIB2 support is a subset of the full language. The Homebrew formula lists two executables, stp and stp_simple; the docs I read only describe stp, so I could not confirm what stp_simple does.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it can solve many kinds of problems generated by program analysis tools, theorem provers, automated bug finders, cryptographic algorithms, intelligent fuzzers and model checkers. The GitHub README describes it as a constraint solver for the same kinds of tools.
brief.how_it_works: STP does word-level preprocessing and then translates what is left to SAT, according to the homepage's Architecture summary. It runs its preprocessing in repeated passes until it reaches a fixed point. The SAT backend is CryptoMiniSat, CaDiCaL, MiniSat, or optionally Incremental Kissat, depending on build and run-time flags.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew is the simple route. Building from source needs git, build-essential, cmake, bison, flex, and python3, and the GitHub README adds libgmp-dev, pkg-config, and zlib1g-dev. The --auto-download flag fetches all dependencies at pinned revisions and builds them, and without it configuration stops and says what to install. The Python example uses 'from stp import *' and needs the stp Python package. The C example needs a compiled libstp and the stp CMake package found by find_package. I did not see any account, licence key, or runtime configuration requirement.
brief.standout: STP is a long-running academic SMT solver with a notable record at SMT-COMP. The homepage lists several first-place finishes in the QF_BV category, from 2006 to 2023. Its Python and C APIs are short, and the homepage's documentation is unusually detailed, with pages on architecture, SAT tuning, and bit-vector abstraction. It is also the solver underneath KLEE, EXE, and several other symbolic-execution and bug-finding tools.
brief.status: maintained. The GitHub repository shows 4,881 commits on master, 592 stars, and 145 forks. The homepage footer reads ©2018-2026, and it lists current 2.x-to-3.x API and SMT-LIB 2.7 compatibility pages. I did not see release dates or a last-commit date in the pages I fetched, so the exact recency of activity is not confirmed.
brief.caveats: The two pages disagree about the default SAT backend. The homepage says the default solver is backed by CaDiCaL, while the GitHub README says CryptoMiniSat is the default backend. Building from source needs several system packages and, with --auto-download, network access during configuration. Only a subset of SMT-LIB2 is supported, and the docs list the accepted logics. The licence is MIT per the homepage. The Windows build exists, but the pages I read only mention it by name. I did not see the Homebrew formula's caveats or a meaning for the stp_simple executable.

entry.title: STP
entry.tldr: A constraint solver that takes logical puzzles about bitvectors and answers satisfiable or not, the same engine that sits under symbolic-execution bug finders like KLEE.
entry.deeper_look:
STP is an SMT solver: you describe a set of constraints over fixed-width integers (bitvectors), arrays, and floating-point numbers, and it tells you whether any assignment of values can satisfy all of them. If one exists, it prints a model. If none does, it says unsat. You hand it a problem as an SMT-LIB2 file or on standard input.

The reason this matters is that a lot of program analysis reduces to exactly this question. Can this input make that branch execute? Can this arithmetic overflow? Can this hash collide? The homepage lists program analysis tools, theorem provers, automated bug finders, cryptographic algorithms, intelligent fuzzers and model checkers as users. It is also the solver underneath KLEE, EXE, and several other symbolic-execution tools.

Inside, STP does word-level preprocessing in repeated passes until it reaches a fixed point, then translates what is left into SAT and hands it to a SAT solver. The backend can be CryptoMiniSat, CaDiCaL, MiniSat, or optionally Incremental Kissat. It also has C, C++, and Python APIs if you want to embed it rather than feed it files.

The door here is the idea of asking a machine to search for inputs that satisfy logic, instead of writing the search yourself. Once you can write a few small bitvector constraints, a lot of reverse engineering and verification papers start to read differently.

entry.caveats: You need to write SMT-LIB2 by hand, only a subset of that language is supported, and the homepage and README disagree on the default SAT backend; I could not confirm what the stp_simple executable does.
